sections.title: Mental model — one template, three disciplines

items: **Boundary discipline**: record-and-continue toward edge (= lower_bound/upper_bound by hand)
**Predicate discipline**: first TRUE in a monotone TTTTFFFF sequence — the master template everything reduces to

blocks.md: **Every binary search = 'find first index where predicate flips'. Exact match and boundaries are special cases. Internalize ONE skeleton:**

blocks.label: the master skeleton (first true)
blocks.py:
lo, hi, ans = lo0, hi0, -1
while lo <= hi:
    mid = (lo + hi) // 2
    if predicate(mid):               # false,false,...,true,true
        ans = mid; hi = mid - 1      # keep earlier truths
    else:
        lo = mid + 1
return ans

blocks.title: Trace: lower_bound of x=8 in {2,4,8,8,10} via predicate a[mid]≥8

items.explain: Strictly-greater flips later; count duplicates = ub−lb.

items.q: Why does predicate MUST be monotone?
options: bisecting a non-monotone flip pattern discards answers

blocks.label: search in rotated sorted array (LC33)
blocks.py:
while lo <= hi:
    mid = (lo + hi) // 2
    if a[mid] == t: return mid
    if a[lo] <= a[mid]:                          # LEFT half sorted?
        if a[lo] <= t < a[mid]: hi = mid - 1
        else: lo = mid + 1
    else:                                        # RIGHT half sorted
        if a[mid] < t <= a[hi]: lo = mid + 1
        else: hi = mid - 1

blocks.label: find minimum in rotated (LC153) & peak (LC162)
blocks.py:
# min in rotated (LC153): compare mid vs RIGHT end
while lo < hi:
    mid = (lo + hi) // 2
    if a[mid] > a[hi]: lo = mid + 1
    else:              hi = mid

# peak element (LC162): climb the uphill side
while lo < hi:
    mid = (lo + hi) // 2
    if a[mid] < a[mid+1]: lo = mid + 1
    else:                 hi = mid

blocks.md: **Converging form `while(lo<hi)`**: never equality-test; hi=mid keeps candidate alive; loop ends lo==hi==answer. Different safety style than L1's exact-match loop — know BOTH.

options: mid<hi ⇒ right side clean-sorted ⇒ min could be mid or left; mid>hi ⇒ rotation point right

items.title: Binary Search (master skeleton rewrite)
items.statement: Reimplement using first-true skeleton with p(i)=a[i]≥target; explain equivalence.

solutionCode.label: first-true skeleton with p(i) = a[i] >= target

followups.q: Why does this need a verification step when plain binary search does not?
followups.a: The predicate only locates where the target *would* be — the first element ≥ it. That slot may hold a larger value if the target is absent. Plain binary search tests equality directly and returns −1 on its own. Separating "find the boundary" from "is it actually there" is what makes one skeleton serve every variant.

followups.q: What must be true of the predicate for this to work?
followups.a: Monotonicity: once it turns true it must stay true across the rest of the range. `a[m] >= target` on a sorted array satisfies that. If the predicate flickers, the search may land in any of the true regions and the result is meaningless — this is the assumption every binary search silently rests on.

items.title: First & Last via predicates
items.statement: lb(x) and lb(x+1)−1 trick OR strict-greater predicate — implement both styles.
hints: Integer overflow on x+1? targets small here.

solutionCode.label: lower_bound and upper_bound from the same skeleton

items.complexity: Two O(log n) searches. Space O(1).

followups.q: Why is upperBound(x) preferable to lowerBound(x+1)?
followups.a: They are equivalent on integers but lowerBound(x+1) overflows when x is INT_MAX, and it is simply wrong for non-integer keys — there is no "next" double or string. Changing `>=` to `>` costs one character and generalises to any ordered type.

followups.q: What sanity check do the two bounds give you?
followups.a: upperBound(x) − lowerBound(x) is the count of elements equal to x, and it must be 0 exactly when x is absent. Any implementation where that identity breaks has an off-by-one — it is the fastest way to test a pair of bound functions.

items.title: Search Insert Position
items.statement: Realize it IS lower_bound — one-liner justification aloud.

solutionCode.label: it IS lower_bound — nothing more to say

followups.q: Give the one-line justification aloud.
followups.a: "Inserting target must keep the array sorted, so it goes immediately before the first element that is not smaller than it — that is exactly lower_bound." Recognising the identity is the answer; re-deriving a bespoke search is the wrong instinct.

followups.q: Where would upper_bound insert instead?
followups.a: After the existing run of equal elements. Both keep the array sorted, so both are "correct" insert positions — the problem specifies lower_bound semantics. For a stable insertion that preserves arrival order among equals, upper_bound is actually the one you want.

items.title: Sqrt(x) hardened
items.statement: Floor sqrt via value-space BS; guard mid*mid overflow.

solutionCode.label: value-space search with the multiplication guarded

followups.q: Why is `mid <= x / mid` safer than `(long long)mid * mid <= x`?
followups.a: Both work, but the division form never produces a value larger than x, so it cannot overflow at any width — it stays correct even if someone later changes the types. The cast version is fine too and is usually faster; the point is that the unguarded `mid * mid` is the one that silently wraps.

followups.q: Why does integer division not break the comparison?
followups.a: x / mid truncates, so the test is slightly conservative — but only at the boundary where mid² and x are within mid of each other, and there the truncation still resolves correctly because both sides are integers. Verify on perfect squares (x = 4, 9, 16) where truncation is exact.

items.title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array I
items.statement: Section code; no duplicates version. Narrate sorted-half logic per step.

solutionCode.label: identify which half is sorted, then test the target against it

followups.q: Why is at least one half always sorted?
followups.a: A rotated sorted array has exactly one break point. Splitting at mid puts that break in one half or the other — never both. So the half without it is fully sorted, and comparing a[lo] against a[mid] identifies which. That guarantee is what lets you keep halving.

followups.q: Why does `a[lo] <= a[mid]` need the equals?
followups.a: When lo == mid (a two-element range) the two are the same element, and a strict `<` would misclassify the left half as unsorted and send the search the wrong way. With no duplicates in the array, `<=` is exact — which is precisely the assumption B206 removes.

items.title: Find Minimum in Rotated II (with duplicates)
items.statement: Duplicates break half-tests — a[mid]==a[hi] ⇒ hi-- safely (can't decide, still shrinks).
hints: Equality branch: hi-- loses AT MOST one copy of answer.
Worst case degrades O(n) — say why honestly.

solutionCode.label: duplicates break the half-test; shrink by one instead

items.complexity: O(log n) average, but O(n) worst case when duplicates dominate. Space O(1).

followups.q: Why is `--hi` safe when a[mid] == a[hi]?
followups.a: If a[hi] equals a[mid], then a[hi] is not a unique minimum — a[mid] holds the same value and survives in the range. So discarding index hi can lose at most one copy of the answer, never the answer itself. It is the standard "cannot decide, but must make progress" move.

followups.q: Be honest about the complexity.
followups.a: On input like [2,2,2,2,1,2] the equality branch fires repeatedly and hi decreases one at a time — O(n). No comparison-based method can do better: duplicates genuinely destroy the information binary search needs. Claiming O(log n) here is the mistake interviewers are listening for.

items.title: Find Peak Element
items.statement: Any peak, imaginary −∞ borders. Converging-form solution.

solutionCode.label: walk uphill; the slope must end at a peak

followups.q: Why must a peak exist in the half you keep?
followups.a: Treat the borders as −∞. If a[mid] < a[mid+1] you are on an ascent; going right you either keep ascending until the −∞ border forces a turn, or you hit a descent — either way a peak exists to the right. The mirror argument covers the descending case. The invariant is "the retained range starts on an ascent or ends on a descent", which forces a peak inside.

followups.q: Prove termination.
followups.a: Each iteration either sets lo = mid+1 (strictly larger) or hi = mid (strictly smaller than the old hi, since mid < hi whenever lo < hi). The range shrinks every step and never skips past the answer, so the loop ends with lo == hi. Using `hi = mid - 1` here would skip a valid peak.

items.title: Peak Index in Mountain Array
items.statement: Strict mountain guarantees unique peak — same slope machinery.

solutionCode.label: same slope machinery; the mountain guarantees uniqueness

followups.q: What does the mountain guarantee buy over B207?
followups.a: Strict increase then strict decrease means exactly one peak, so the answer is unique rather than "any peak". The code is identical — but B207 may return different valid answers on the same input, while this one is deterministic. Knowing the code is the same is more useful than treating them as two problems.

followups.q: What breaks if the array has a plateau?
followups.a: With a[mid] == a[mid+1] the slope test cannot tell which way to go, and the search can walk away from the true peak. The mountain constraint forbids plateaus, which is exactly why the constraint is stated. On general arrays with plateaus, no O(log n) solution exists.

items.title: Search a 2D Matrix (globally sorted)
items.statement: One binary search over virtual 1D space.
hints: r = idx / cols, c = idx % cols.

solutionCode.label: treat the matrix as one flat sorted array

followups.q: What property makes flattening legal?
followups.a: The whole matrix is sorted in row-major order — every element of row i is smaller than the first element of row i+1. That makes the flattened view a genuinely sorted 1D array. B210 drops this guarantee, and the technique dies with it.

followups.q: Why divide and mod by cols rather than rows?
followups.a: Row-major layout means consecutive flat indices walk across a row, so the column is the fast-varying coordinate: col = idx % cols, row = idx / cols. Swapping them silently reads the wrong cell on any non-square matrix — and works on square ones, which is why it survives testing.

items.title: Search a 2D Matrix II (staircase)
items.statement: Rows+cols sorted only. Top-right elimination walk.
hints: Explain why binary search per row is worse (n log n vs m+n).

solutionCode.label: start top-right; every comparison kills a row or a column

items.complexity: O(m + n) — each step eliminates a full row or column. Space O(1).

followups.q: Why the top-right corner specifically?
followups.a: It is the only corner where the two moves are unambiguous: going left strictly decreases, going down strictly increases. From the top-left both moves increase, so a "too big" result gives you no way to eliminate anything. Bottom-left works too, by symmetry.

followups.q: Why is binary search per row worse?
followups.a: That is m searches at log n each — O(m log n). The staircase is O(m + n). For a 1000×1000 matrix that is 10,000 versus 2,000 steps. The staircase wins because one comparison eliminates an entire row or column, while a per-row search throws away the information from the previous row.

items.title: Single Element in Sorted Pairs Array
items.statement: Pairs adjacent until lone element. Parity predicate bisects.
hints: Break flips parity — first violation = answer zone.

solutionCode.label: parity predicate: pairs are intact left of the break

followups.q: What is the monotone predicate here?
followups.a: "The pairing is broken at or before index mid." It is false for every index left of the lone element and true from there on — exactly the false...false true...true shape the L2 skeleton needs. Naming the predicate is what turns a fiddly parity puzzle into the standard search.

followups.q: Why does the array length have to be odd?
followups.a: Every value appears twice except one, so the total is 2k + 1. An even length would mean the input violates the premise. It is worth stating as a precondition — and it is why the final range always converges to a single valid index rather than an empty one.

Min-rotated & peak use converging while(lo<hi), hi=mid style
Duplicates degrade rotated-min to O(n) worst — honest answer
2D choice: global sort ⇒ flatten log(mn); partial sort ⇒ staircase m+n
Pair-parity bisect finds lone element (mid^1 partner check)
